At the kitchen table, a woman tests a pen on the edge of an electricity bill. It makes a faint groove, then a blue loop. She moves the mug to cover a damp ring and begins again on the good paper. Before she has written a sentence, the letter has acquired a setting: Tuesday, rain, the boiler clicking behind her. Her brother will receive only the paper. Still, something of this small arrangement will travel with it. The crooked first line records the position of her wrist. The larger gap before his name holds a hesitation he may never notice.

People who keep letters often remember their envelopes almost as clearly as their contents. The thin foreign paper, the address crowded into one corner, the familiar mistake in the postcode. A particular hand can announce someone before any name does. The letters lean forward as though impatient, or stand apart with the careful spacing of fence posts. This recognition feels close to hearing footsteps in a hall. We know the person through a repeated movement. Even the faults belong to them. An uneven capital, copied badly at school seventy years earlier, can carry more intimacy than the words that follow.

The writer also meets these movements, although from the other side. A hand grows tired. The pen catches where a crumb has dented the page. There is time to reconsider a complaint while searching for a word. Perhaps the complaint stays. Perhaps the writer remembers that the person who caused it has been sleeping badly since the operation. Paper does not make anyone kinder. But its small inconveniences can give another thought room to arrive. The sentence cannot vanish with one touch. A line through it leaves the first feeling visible beneath the second, like something seen through shallow water.

Then comes the peculiar interval after posting. The letter lies somewhere the writer cannot see: beneath other envelopes, inside a sack, against a sorting machine. For several days, the words belong fully to neither person. A question travels without collecting an answer. Some people find relief in that interval. They have spoken, and now they must leave the other person alone. No small symbol confirms that the envelope has opened. The silence may mean illness, distraction, resentment, or simply another long week full of errands. Waiting can become a modest exercise in admitting that another life continues beyond our view.

Of course, waiting has never felt equally gentle to everyone. A letter can spend weeks in a prison office before its intended reader sees it. A family can wait beside an empty letterbox for news that would change every plan. Postage costs money, and so does the spare hour. Painful fingers may refuse the work altogether. Anyone praising handwriting should remember those for whom a keyboard makes expression possible. The affection for paper becomes less interesting when it demands that everyone share it. Its pleasures remain particular, shaped by the body, the circumstances, and the person we hope will answer.

Often there is little news. The beans have failed again. A neighbour has painted his gate a green that nobody can agree about. Someone encloses a recipe, although the recipient has made the same cake for thirty years. These details might seem too slight to justify an envelope. Yet their slightness can be the point. The writer has noticed something and chosen someone to tell. The green gate becomes a shared possession. Across the distance, two people briefly occupy the same ordinary afternoon, with its bad harvest and its unnecessary cake. Neither needs to explain why this should be enough.

There is also the pleasure of making something small and complete. The writer folds the sheet into thirds and presses each crease with a thumbnail. A pressed leaf needs its own protection. A photograph makes the envelope bulge. These decisions give affection a few practical jobs. Buy stamps. Find the address. Check that the flap holds. Love can become abstract through repetition, especially between people who already know the familiar declarations. An envelope offers another vocabulary. The effort need not be impressive. Sometimes its value lies in being slightly troublesome, and in someone having accepted that trouble for your sake.

Later, the letter may lose its envelope and enter a drawer. There it sits among batteries, foreign coins, and instructions for an appliance that has already broken. Nobody intended to create an archive. Years pass before someone reads it again. The news has expired, but the handwriting has acquired a force the writer could not have planned. A dead father asks whether the roof still leaks. His concern survives in a question nobody needs to answer. The reader touches the place where the pen pressed hardest, and finds a small ridge on the reverse. Such meetings can happen without warning.

But the woman at the kitchen table is not thinking about drawers or the people who will open them. Her tea has cooled. She has reached the bottom of the page and still needs to mention the dog. She turns the sheet sideways and writes along the margin. Her brother will have to turn it too. For a moment, his hands will follow the decision made by hers. She adds that the dog now refuses the old path beside the river. Then she remembers one more thing and squeezes it beneath her signature: the water is low enough to cross.

A library that closes at six serves the public until the moment much of the public becomes free. For someone who finishes work at five, the journey home can consume the remaining hour. Collect a child, prepare dinner, and the chance disappears. The building may stand at the center of town, but its timetable places it beyond reach. Public libraries should remain open until ten on weekday evenings, with schedules adapted to local demand. This should be a normal public service, supported by stable funding. Access means little when a locked door separates people from services their taxes help provide.

We often discuss library access as a question of distance. Can residents walk to a branch, or reach one by bus? Time deserves equal attention. A nearby library can remain effectively unavailable to a cleaner, a shop assistant, or a parent working long shifts. People with flexible jobs can arrange daytime visits more easily. People with less control over their schedules cannot. Closing early therefore distributes a shared service unevenly, even when everyone holds the same library card. Evening hours would give more residents a practical opportunity to use what already belongs to them. That is a matter of fairness.

Consider a teenager who shares a bedroom with younger siblings. At home, homework competes with conversation, television, and the ordinary noise of family life. A quiet desk can change the evening. Consider an adult studying for a qualification after a full working day. Reliable internet and a librarian who can find suitable materials can make that effort more manageable. Neither person needs an elaborate new government program. Both need an existing building to welcome them when they can actually arrive. We already invest in books, computers, desks, and trained staff. Early closing leaves those public resources idle during useful hours.

The internet does not remove this need. A phone can display an application form without making that form easy to complete. A household connection does not guarantee a quiet room, a printer, or help with an unfamiliar website. Libraries provide those practical supports without requiring a purchase. Their evening role also extends beyond work and study. A retired neighbor may want company after dinner. A reader may simply want an hour among books. These uses deserve respect. Public institutions should support ordinary pleasures as well as urgent needs. Reading for enjoyment requires no economic justification before it earns public space.

The strongest objection is money, and supporters of longer hours must answer it honestly. Many libraries already struggle to maintain their collections and retain enough staff. Another four hours can require additional wages, lighting, heating, cleaning, and security. A city cannot spend the same dollar twice. If evening opening means fewer librarians during busy mornings, the change could harm the people it intends to help. If officials demand longer hours without additional funding, they merely transfer the cost to exhausted workers. Libraries should reject that bargain. A credible proposal must include the money and staffing that safe evening service requires.

That expense does not settle the question. Councils routinely pay to keep public facilities useful during the hours residents need them. They should assess libraries by the same standard. Buildings and collections already represent substantial investments. Additional opening hours can increase their value, although the local costs will vary. The choice deserves a place in budget debates alongside other services, with its price clearly stated. Officials should identify what they would fund less generously to support evening access. Supporters must defend that choice openly. Pretending the service costs nothing would weaken an argument that can stand on its public benefits.

Implementation should reflect geography and demand. A large city could begin with several branches that residents can reach easily by public transport. A small town might extend hours on three dependable evenings before expanding further. Consistency matters because people need to plan visits around jobs, classes, and family responsibilities. A confusing rotation of late nights would frustrate that purpose. Councils should consult residents who rarely visit, including those whose schedules currently prevent them from entering. Asking only existing daytime visitors would miss much of the need. A useful consultation asks when people could attend and what currently prevents their visits.

Staff must help design the service. Evening work affects their families, transport, and safety, just as closing times affect library users. Councils should provide fair pay, adequate staffing, and predictable schedules. They should also assess entrances, lighting, emergency procedures, and transport after closing. Some branches may need security staff or links with outreach services. Librarians cannot replace social workers, and longer opening must never become an excuse to ignore that distinction. These requirements belong in the original budget. A library serves its community through the people who work there. Good working conditions help staff provide the service their community deserves.

Councils should test extended hours over a full year and publish the results. Count visits, computer use, attendance at events, and requests for help. Ask whether evening visitors can also attend during the library’s original opening hours. Compare the additional expense with other ways of improving access, including weekend opening. Some locations may justify fewer late evenings. Others may reveal demand that early closing concealed. Adjust the schedule when the evidence warrants it. Still, attendance alone cannot capture every benefit. A quiet hour can matter enormously to someone with nowhere else to study. Numbers should inform judgment without replacing it.

The larger question concerns how we organize public life. We expect adults to work, students to learn, and families to manage increasingly complicated schedules. Our public services should recognize those demands. An evening library offers a place where a person can enter without buying anything or explaining their income. It gives a town somewhere to read, think, seek help, and share space after the working day. That opportunity deserves a serious claim on public funds. Councils should budget for it, staff it properly, and make it dependable. When residents have time to enter, the library door should still be open.

Raft keeps a group of servers consistent by having them agree on a sequence of commands. Each server stores that sequence in a log and applies committed commands to its state machine. One server acts as the leader and coordinates this work. Leader election lets the group choose that server and replace it after failures. The challenge is to choose a leader safely despite delayed messages, failed servers, and networks that can separate healthy machines.

Each server has one of three roles: follower, candidate, or leader. A follower responds to requests from leaders and candidates. A candidate asks other servers to elect it as leader. A leader sends log entries to followers and coordinates their replication. Servers normally start as followers. These roles can change repeatedly during the lifetime of a cluster. A server does not need special hardware or a permanent priority to become the next leader in Raft.

Raft divides time into numbered terms. Think of a term as an election round, not a fixed duration. Each term begins with an election attempt and can have at most one elected leader. Some terms end without electing anyone. Servers include their current term in protocol messages. These numbers help servers recognize outdated information. Terms act like a logical clock. They order leadership attempts without requiring synchronized clocks or agreement about the current wall clock time.

When a server receives a message with a higher term, it updates its term and becomes a follower. This rule applies even if the server currently considers itself the leader. Requests from older terms are rejected. Each server persistently stores its current term and its vote for that term before responding. Persistence matters because a restart must not erase these facts. Otherwise, a server could forget its previous vote and vote twice within one term.

Leaders send regular heartbeats to followers, even when clients submit no commands. In Raft, a heartbeat is an AppendEntries request containing no log entries. It tells followers that a leader is still communicating with them. Ordinary AppendEntries requests also serve this purpose. A follower resets its election timer when it receives valid communication from the current leader. Heartbeats reduce unnecessary elections, but they do not prove that every server can communicate with every other server.

A follower starts an election when its election timer expires without suitable leader communication. This election timeout is longer than the normal interval between heartbeats. It gives routine message delays some room before the follower suspects a failure. The timeout cannot distinguish a crashed leader from a slow or unreachable one. It is a suspicion mechanism. Engineers must choose timeout settings that accommodate network latency, scheduling delays, and pauses in server execution under expected load.

To start an election, a follower becomes a candidate and increments its current term. It votes for itself, resets its election timer, and sends RequestVote requests to the other servers. These requests include its term and information about its last log entry. A candidate wins when it receives votes from a majority of the cluster, including its own vote. For example, a cluster with five servers requires three votes, while three servers require two votes.

A server grants at most one candidate its vote during a term. It also requires the candidate’s log to be at least as current as its own. Raft first compares the terms of their last log entries. The higher term indicates the more current log. If those terms match, the higher last entry index wins. This check helps preserve committed commands across leadership changes. Granting a vote also resets the server’s timer for starting elections.

The majority requirement explains why two candidates cannot both win the same term. Any two majorities of the same cluster share at least one server. That shared server would have to vote for both candidates, which Raft forbids. Once elected, a leader immediately sends heartbeats to establish its authority. A candidate becomes a follower when it receives an AppendEntries request from a leader in its own term. Higher terms also cause candidates to become followers.

An election can fail when several followers become candidates at nearly the same time. For example, three candidates in a cluster of five servers might receive two, two, and one votes. Nobody has the required three votes. This result is called a split vote. Candidates cannot collect another vote from a server that already chose someone else in that term. When its election timer expires, a candidate increases its term and begins another election attempt.

Raft reduces split votes by randomizing election timeouts. Each server chooses its timeout independently from a configured range and chooses again for subsequent elections. Usually, one follower reaches its timeout early enough to request votes before others become candidates. Once elected, it sends heartbeats that prevent competing elections. Randomization also separates repeated attempts after a split vote. It improves the chance of progress, but cannot guarantee success during arbitrary message delays or continuing network failures.

A network partition can leave an old leader isolated while a majority elects a replacement. The old leader might still believe it leads, but it cannot commit new commands without majority agreement. When it learns the higher term, it becomes a follower. If no connected group contains a majority, Raft cannot elect a new leader. This tradeoff protects consistency: the cluster can pause progress until enough servers can communicate and establish a legitimate leader again.

Nora held the cake box level while the ferry rolled beneath her feet. The last crossing left at eleven forty, and the crew had already raised the ramp. Through the cabin windows, she saw a cleaner pushing water across the empty terminal floor.

The only dry bench outside stood beside the engine housing. A man sat at one end, his knees pressed against a canvas bag.

“Is that space free?”

He moved the bag between his boots.

“Unless the cake needs it.”

“The cake has enjoyed enough attention.”

She sat, keeping the box on her lap as they left shore.

For a while, they watched the city shrink. Orange lights stretched across the black water, then broke beneath the wake. Somewhere above them, a loose fitting tapped against a rail.

“Birthday?” the man asked.

“Retirement.”

“Congratulations.”

“That seems to be the agreed response.”

He glanced at her, then smiled when she smiled.

“Was it a good day?”

Nora considered the paper banner, the warm wine, the headmaster reading her name from a card.

“Parts of it.”

“What did you do?”

“School dinners. Thirty years.”

“That is a lot of dinners.”

“Yes,” she said. “It was.”

The engines took them east.

He introduced himself as Daniel. His bag contained work shoes, he explained, and a shirt that smelled of popcorn.

“The cinema by the station. I clean after the final screening.”

“I used to go there.”

“It still has the terrible carpet.”

“Red flowers?”

“Possibly flowers. Nobody can prove it.”

She laughed and felt the box shift against her.

He checked his phone. A photograph filled the screen: a baby asleep beneath a yellow blanket.

“Yours?”

“Eight weeks.”

“Are you getting any sleep?”

“Some. Usually when somebody needs me awake.”

He typed a reply, then returned the phone to his pocket.

Nora rested her palms on the cardboard lid. All evening, people asked about her plans.

“Travel,” they suggested. “A garden. You could finally learn Italian.”

She had agreed that these things sounded pleasant.

Beside her, Daniel studied the lights along the dark shore.

“What happens on Monday?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“That sounds good.”

“I always caught the five fifteen. Before that, the four fifty, when they changed the timetable.”

He waited.

“I keep thinking somebody will telephone because they cannot find the big saucepan.”

“Will they?”

“No. I showed everyone where it was.”

She pressed a finger into the lid.

A gust lifted the edge of her coat. Daniel trapped it against the bench before it touched a puddle.

“Thank you.”

“Strong wind tonight.”

She opened the box. Pink icing covered the cake, and someone had piped THANK YOU NORA across it. The knife and two paper plates lay underneath a napkin.

“They bought it from the supermarket,” she said.

“Is that bad?”

“No. I like this one.”

She rarely bought anything that she could make at home.

“Would you like some?”

“I would.”

She cut through the lettering, separating her name from the thanks.

The ferry sounded its horn.

Daniel balanced his plate against the bag. He ate with his fingers, carefully catching crumbs in his other hand.

“My wife likes the icing best,” he said. “She leaves the sponge.”

“An inefficient arrangement.”

“I eat the sponge.”

“Then you chose well.”

He smiled with his mouth full.

Nora took a bite. The cake tasted of sugar and lemon flavouring. After an evening of handshakes, photographs, and speeches, hunger reached her.

“I ate nothing at the party,” she said.

“Too busy?”

“Cutting cake.”

Daniel looked at her plate.

“Take another piece.”

“I have barely started this one.”

“There is time.”

The ferry cleared the harbour wall. Waves slapped its side, and Nora braced her shoes against the deck. Daniel steadied the box between them.

For several minutes, neither spoke. She heard him lick icing from his thumb.

“Sometimes I stay here instead of going inside,” he said. “Even in winter.”

“To avoid the carpet?”

“To sit where nobody needs anything.”

She thought of the baby beneath its blanket.

“Just for the crossing,” he added.

“I understand,” she said.

He nodded. Beyond the railing, a channel marker flashed green. Nora watched it disappear behind them, then waited for the next one.

“Will you miss it?” Daniel asked.

“Some children said thank you every day. Others learned after a few years.”

“The children, then.”

“And the women I worked with. And knowing exactly how much rice to put in the pot.”

“How much?”

“Depends who is eating.”

He laughed.

She turned her plate towards the light. A crescent of icing remained. She scraped it with her finger.

“I will not miss the rice,” she decided. “But I might miss knowing.”

Daniel considered this.

“I check whether the baby is breathing about twenty times a night.”

“That part gets easier.”

“I hope so.”

The island appeared as a low bank of windows. Daniel brushed crumbs from his trousers and reached for his bag.

Nora cut another piece, larger than the first.

“For your wife.”

“She would like that.”

“Take the rest, if you want.”

She made the offer before she even thought about it.

Daniel glanced into the box.

“Do you want the rest?”

She looked at the uneven pink edge, the exposed layers of pale sponge.

“Yes,” she said. “Actually, I do.”

“Then I had better leave it.”

She wrapped his piece in the napkin. He held it flat against his palm.

They stood when the engine slowed. Along the quay, the night crew waited beside a stack of ropes.

“Enjoy your Monday, Nora.”

“I expect I shall be awake at four.”

“You can stay in bed.”

“I might.”

She knew she probably would not. There would be gulls arguing on the roof and milk in the fridge. She could make breakfast when she wanted it.

At the ramp, Daniel raised his parcel before turning towards the waiting buses.

Nora carried the box through the gate. The wind pressed at her back. She had half a cake left, enough for several days.

After a week of trains, desk work, and evening walks, its appeal feels clear. These headphones put comfort and an easy listening experience ahead of flashy design. The Q3 rarely feels luxurious. It does, however, feel carefully judged for people who want useful headphones without paying for every possible extra.

On busier rock recordings, bass guitars sometimes crowd the lower notes of male voices. The companion app helps here. Reducing bass by two steps gives instruments more space without making the presentation thin. Treble stays smooth rather than sharp, which makes long sessions pleasant. For an office or a cool train carriage, though, the fit remains comfortable and stable without constant adjustment.

Voices still penetrate, and sudden sounds remain obvious, so the Q3 cannot create complete silence. Transparency mode is useful for announcements, although nearby speech sounds slightly metallic. 1. **Acknowledge the alert.** Record the cluster, affected standby, alert start time, and current lag in the incident log. Check whether customers receive stale results or read errors.

2. **Protect affected reads.** Remove the standby from read traffic if stale results affect customers. Route reads only to a healthy destination with spare capacity. Do not promote a standby solely to clear this alert.

3. **Validate the measurement.** Check that the heartbeat advances on the primary. Check monitoring freshness and clock synchronization. A failed heartbeat job can produce this alert without a replication failure.

   Do not use `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` alone to confirm lag. That value increases during idle periods, even when the standby has no outstanding transactions.

4. **Inspect replication on the primary.** Use the approved monitoring account:

   ```sql
   SELECT application_name,
          client_addr,
          state,
          sync_state,
          sent_lsn,
          write_lsn,
          flush_lsn,
          replay_lsn,
          pg_wal_lsn_diff(
            pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn
          ) AS pending_bytes
   FROM pg_stat_replication;
   ```

   Identify the affected standby by its registered name and address. A missing row means the primary has no active WAL sender for that standby.

5. **Inspect the affected standby.**

   ```sql
   SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby,
          pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received_lsn,
          pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() AS replayed_lsn,
          pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state() AS pause_state;
   ```

   If `is_standby` is false, stop corrective actions and escalate. The server role differs from the expected topology.

6. **Repeat both samples after 30 seconds.** Use separate transactions so each sample receives fresh statistics. Log sequence numbers, or LSNs, identify positions in the write-ahead log (WAL).

   If received WAL trails the primary, investigate delivery or write capacity. If received WAL advances but replay stalls, investigate replay delays. If both advance slowly, compare WAL production with standby processing capacity.

   Byte differences show outstanding WAL volume, not elapsed time. PostgreSQL’s [replication statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html#MONITORING-PG-STAT-REPLICATION-VIEW) describe `replay_lag` as recent replay delay, not recovery time. A null value does not prove that replication is healthy.

7. **Compare supporting evidence.** Check CPU, storage latency, free space, network errors, WAL production, and database logs. Compare the alert start time with deployments, bulk imports, backups, and scheduled reports.

The public library is one of the few civic rooms left that does not ask you to buy something before you sit down. It is also, in too many cities, a room that locks its doors just as the people who need it most are getting off work. A branch that closes at five or six does not fail because librarians are lazy or because the books have lost their audience. It fails the schedule of ordinary life. If a city can keep one promise to people who work for a living, it should be this: the library stays open into the evening.

That is not a romantic claim about the smell of paper. It is a claim about time. The hours between nine and five are already spoken for. They belong to employers, to school, to the second job, to the bus that runs late, to the child who has to be collected. A parent who stocks shelves until seven cannot use a reading room that shut at six. A student who shares a two-bedroom apartment with three roommates does not get quiet until everyone else is asleep, and by then the only free internet left in the neighborhood is a closed building with the lights off. We have arranged the one public good designed for study, job applications, and unhurried reading so that it is available mainly to people whose days are already free.

Evening hours repair that without inventing a new institution. They take a building the city already owns, a staff it already employs, and a collection it already paid for, and they put those assets on the clock of the people who fund them. Anyone who has stood in a branch at 8:15 knows what later hours produce. The room fills with people finishing résumés, teenagers doing homework away from a loud house, new arrivals practicing English, and older patrons who would rather not walk home in the dark from a five o'clock closing. The demand was never absent. It was locked out.

The objection that deserves a straight answer is money. Later hours cost money. They mean more wages, more security, more heat and light, and, in buildings that are already tired, more wear. Library budgets have been cut, frozen, and "right-sized" for years, and directors are right to flinch at any proposal that sounds like a wish list. A serious case for evening hours has to survive that flinch.

It survives because the alternative is more expensive in a way budget hearings rarely count. A library open only in the daytime has already paid for the building, the collection, the catalog, and the broadband, and then refused the hours when working households can use them. That is not thrift. That is a stranded asset. The marginal cost of two or three more open hours is real, and a city should publish it in plain figures beside the cost of a new branch. If the figures are too high, the honest move is to choose, not to shrug and close at five. Close a little earlier one morning if the numbers demand it. Share evening duty across a system so that not every branch stays late every night, but every neighborhood has one that does. Staff the late shift as a normal schedule, not as leftover overtime piled on people who already worked a full day. Security is a design problem: sight lines, a single public entrance, a guard where the numbers say one is needed, and the same rules after dark that apply at noon. Evening access is part of the service, the way a late train is part of a transit system.

There is a second version of the money objection that is really an argument about fairness inside the building. Evening hours, critics say, will pull staff away from children's story time, reference desks, and the morning programs that retirees rely on. That worry is legitimate if a city simply stretches the same small crew across a longer day and calls it innovation. It is not legitimate as a reason to keep the doors shut. Story time at ten in the morning and a quiet room at eight at night are not rivals. They are the same mission meeting different lives. A branch that can do only one of them should say so, and should say which residents it has decided not to serve. Most branches, given a schedule written on purpose, can do both.

The long table still matters when the apartment is a bedroom with a television in it. Print still matters to the patron who does not trust a screen with a form that decides the rent. Those needs do not expire at dusk. They get sharper, because dusk is when the rest of the day's rooms have already asked for a wallet.

Shift workers pay it on the weeks they are free only after supper. A library that cannot be bothered to be open when they are free has not made a neutral budget decision. It has said that their time is less civic than someone else's.

Keep the lights on until nine. Publish the cost. Staff the shift properly, and judge the result by who walks in after supper, not by who was already there at three in the afternoon. The books can wait on the shelf. The people cannot.

Each follower runs an election timer that starts when the server becomes a follower. The timer restarts if AppendEntries arrives from the current leader, and it restarts if the follower grants a vote. If the timer expires, the follower has seen neither, so it starts an election.

Each timer is a fresh random draw, so servers rarely expire together, and the shortest draw must exceed broadcast time. On expiry the follower adds one to its term, becomes a candidate, and votes for itself. It stores the term and the vote on stable storage, then sends RequestVote in parallel to every other server. The message carries the new term, the candidate id, and the index and term of its last log entry. It then starts another random timer. If that timer expires and no one has a majority, the candidate repeats this in the next term.

A server grants the vote only if every check passes. The candidate's term is at least the server's term. The server has not already voted for someone else in this term. The candidate's log is at least as up to date as the server's log. The log with the higher term on its last entry is more up to date. If the last terms match, an equal or longer log passes. A server missing committed entries therefore cannot win and overwrite them. The server stores the term and the vote on stable storage before it replies, and a restart still shows that vote as spent.

The candidate counts its own vote toward a majority of the configured cluster. Five servers need three votes, so a partition of two cannot elect a leader and the other three can. The winner becomes leader and sends heartbeats immediately. AppendEntries from an existing leader at an equal or higher term also ends the attempt, and the candidate becomes a follower. If the timer expires with no majority, the result is a split vote.

The config format is TOML. tidewatch loads `~/.config/tidewatch/config.toml`. A `tidewatch.toml` file in the current directory overrides keys that it sets. `TIDEWATCH_CONFIG` selects another path.

```
poll_interval = "30m"
cache_ttl = "2h"
timezone = "harbour"
units = "metres"

[[harbours]]
    name = "plymouth"
    station = "ukho:ply-01"
    label = "Devonport"

[[harbours]]
    name = "falmouth"
    station = "ukho:fal-01"
    label = "Falmouth"

[[harbours]]
    name = "st-marys"
    station = "ukho:stm-01"
    label = "St Mary's"
```

`poll_interval` is the pause between fetches in `watch`. The default is 30 minutes. `cache_ttl` is how long a normal run reuses a table. The default is 2 hours.

`timezone` takes `harbour`, `utc`, or an IANA name such as `Europe/London`. `units` takes `metres` or `feet`.

`station` is `provider:id`. Built-in providers are `ukho`, `noaa`, and `shom`. The id is that provider's station code. A wrong code is the usual cause of an empty tide.

If a provider requires a key, set `TIDEWATCH_PROVIDER_KEY` in the environment. tidewatch reads the variable at startup. The key stays in the environment.

**The shell cannot find the command.** The install directory is not on `PATH`. Run `command -v tidewatch`. If the result is empty, open a new shell.

**`unknown harbour`.** The name does not match a `name` key. Run `tidewatch list` and copy the key. The match is case sensitive.

**`station returned no events`.** The station id is wrong, or the provider has no rows for the next 48 hours. Compare the id with the provider catalogue. Many secondary ports have no table. Use the standard port from the sailing directions.

**Times are an hour off.** With `timezone = "harbour"`, each station uses the zone published with its table. A fixed IANA name puts every harbour in that one zone. The difference appears at the BST and GMT change.

**`rate limited`, or the fetched time is old.** A loop is calling `tidewatch refresh` too often. Normal runs should honour `cache_ttl`. After HTTP 429, tidewatch waits 10 minutes and serves the last good table.

**No output, exit code 0.** The harbour list is empty. An empty list is valid TOML and still exits 0. Add at least one `[[harbours]]` entry.

**Checksum failed during install.** Do not run that binary. Download the archive and the checksum file again. A mismatch means the download is not the release file.

Exit status is 0 on success, 1 for a bad argument or an unknown harbour, 2 for a config error, and 3 when the provider failed and no cached table is left.

       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication
ORDER BY application_name;

SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_age,

The drawer sticks before it opens, and when it does, the smell comes up first: cedar liner, old paper, the faint mineral ghost of ink. Inside is a shoebox my grandmother covered in wallpaper sometime in the sixties, and inside the box are letters, bundled with a rubber band that snapped years ago and left two brittle commas of itself among the envelopes. I know these letters. I have read them in the way you read things you are not supposed to keep rereading, and still, when the drawer sticks and gives, I feel something in me adjust its posture.

Her hand was a slope to the right, the letters leaning like people walking into wind. She wrote on airmail paper so thin you could read the next sheet through it, and she never crossed anything out. That is the part I return to. Not the news in the letters, which was ordinary, the price of oranges, a neighbor's surgery, rain. What I return to is the absence of error, or rather the refusal to acknowledge it. Somewhere in the third bundle she writes my uncle's name with the wrong initial, a D where there should be an R, and she simply finishes the word and goes on. The mistake is still there, sixty years old, dry as a pressed flower. A text message would have eaten it. Here it sits, proof that a person was moving through time at the speed of her own hand and did not stop to fix herself.

I started writing letters again during a winter when the power kept going out. The house would go dark and the router's little constellation would die, and after the first hour of phone-battery rationing I would light a candle and find, with nothing left to refresh, that I had things to say to people. Real things, it turned out, the kind that had been dissolving into the general noise for years. I wrote to a friend in Lisbon who I had not spoken to properly in three years. I wrote to my aunt. I wrote to a man I owed an apology, and the apology took four drafts, and each draft existed, physically, and had to be dealt with, folded into the woodstove or kept, and the keeping or burning was itself part of the deciding. You cannot burn a draft of an email. There is nothing to burn, and so the deciding never quite happens, and the sending is too easy, and the apology arrives weighing nothing.

The pen matters more than I expected it to. Mine is a cheap fountain pen, the kind students use in Germany, and it scratches on the upstroke if I hold it wrong, which I do. The scratch is audible. Writing a letter, I can hear myself think, literally, a small rasping like a mouse in a wall. I have come to distrust silence in writing. The blinking cursor makes no sound and forgives everything, and I have noticed that what I type in silence comes out smooth and false, committee prose, while what I write with the scratch comes out crooked and mine. Other letter writers I have asked say versions of the same thing. A woman I know writes only with a pencil because, she says, she likes that it gets lighter in her hand as the letter goes on, the point wearing down, the words toward the end slightly fatter and darker. Her letters record their own fatigue. She can see where she tired.

Then there is the envelope, the stamp, the walk. Our mailbox is a quarter mile down the road and the walk back, empty-handed, is longer than the walk out. You have given something up. It will take four days to reach Lisbon, maybe six, and during those days the letter exists somewhere, in a sack, on a plane, in the hands of a Portuguese postal worker I will never meet, and the friend does not have it yet, and I cannot recall it, cannot add a follow-up, cannot soften it. The letter is gone in a way nothing digital is ever gone. I think people write letters by hand, partly, to recover that gone-ness, to say a thing and have it leave. We are drowning in retrievable words. Everything is saved and nothing is sent.

The reply, when it comes, arrives at the speed of weather. My friend in Lisbon writes on the backs of exhibition postcards, cramped, running out of room exactly where the interesting part starts, so that every letter ends in a parenthetical sprint. I hold the card he held. He pressed on this paper and the paper pressed back and it kept the shape of his pressure, the dents of his pen readable by fingertip in the right light. This is the thing people mean when they say letters are personal, though they usually say it vaguely, sentimentally. It is not vague at all. It is mechanical. Force, applied to a surface, at a distance of a thousand kilometers and six days, reaching my thumb. No screen does this. The screen shows me what he wrote; the card shows me that he was there.

I do not think the hand-written letter will survive as a common thing. It barely is one now. The shoebox in my drawer is an archive of a world that has already ended, and my own letters, stacked unsent or returned with wrong addresses, are a small eccentricity, like keeping chickens. But on the dark winter evenings when the candle is lit and the pen scratches and the mouse in the wall keeps time, I am not being eccentric. I am doing one of the oldest things a person can do: making a mark that cannot be unmade, and trusting the weather to carry it.

# The lights should stay on at the library

Every weekday at five or six in the evening, in towns across the country, the same quiet eviction takes place. A librarian makes an announcement, chairs get stacked, and a building full of people who have nowhere else to go files out into the parking lot. The students working on laptops, the job seekers filling out applications, the parents with restless toddlers, the retirees reading the newspaper: all of them leave, and the lights go dark on the most democratic institution most of us will ever use.

This is a choice, not a law of nature. Public libraries should stay open late into the evening, until nine or ten at night, and the reasons reach well past the shelves of books.

Start with the people who work. A library that closes at five is a library for people who do not have jobs, which is a strange design for an institution that exists to serve everyone. The nurse finishing a shift, the warehouse worker on an evening schedule, the parent who cannot leave the office before six: these people pay for the library through their taxes and then find the door locked when they finally have an hour to spare. Evening hours are not a luxury add-on. They are the difference between a public service and a service for the publicly leisured.

Students feel the closing time most sharply. Not every teenager has a quiet bedroom, a desk, and reliable internet. Many share apartments with siblings, work evening jobs themselves, or live in homes where concentration is impossible. For them, the library is the one place where homework actually gets done. When it closes early, we are telling the students who need help most that their education matters only during business hours. Teachers assign more online work every year. The gap between the student with a home office and the student without one grows wider each semester. A late library is one of the cheapest interventions we have against that gap, and it requires no new curriculum, no new technology, and no new staff training. It requires keeping the door open.

Then there is the simple matter of physical space. Most towns have steadily lost the places where a person can exist without buying something. The mall is gone or dying. The coffee shop wants you to order. Parks close at dusk and are useless in January or in a heat wave. The library is nearly the last indoor public space where presence is free, where nobody checks whether you have purchased anything, and where staying for three hours is normal rather than suspicious. In the evening that function matters most, because evening is when loneliness bites, when teenagers look for somewhere to be, and when people in crisis need warmth, light, and a human face. We spend enormous sums worrying about what young people do after dark. Keeping the library open is one answer that costs a fraction of a new police initiative.

The strongest objection, and it deserves a serious answer, is money. Library budgets are tight everywhere. Keeping a branch open four extra hours a night means paying staff, heating and cooling the building, and covering security. Opponents ask a fair question: why spend scarce funds on hours when attendance may be thin?

The answer has several parts. First, the assumption of thin attendance is wrong wherever evening hours have actually been tried. Libraries that extend into the evening consistently report that the after-dinner crowd arrives: working adults who could never come at two in the afternoon, students after sports practice, families after dinner. You cannot measure demand for a service that does not exist. Low evening attendance at a closed building proves nothing.

Second, the marginal cost of evening hours is smaller than critics suggest, because the expensive parts of a library already exist. The building is built. The collection is purchased. The catalog system runs around the clock anyway. What extended hours add is staffing and utilities on a structure that otherwise sits dark and unused, which is its own kind of waste. Many systems have found savings by shifting hours rather than adding them: opening later on quiet weekday mornings, when foot traffic is lightest, and staying open later in exchange. The total budget stays nearly flat while the service reaches people it never reached before.

Third, and most important, the cost argument weighs only one side of the ledger. A library open until ten is a quiet form of youth programming, adult education, job search assistance, and shelter during extreme weather, all at once, all under one roof that the public already owns. Buy those services separately, through new programs and new buildings, and the price would be many times higher. The evening library is not a new expense so much as fuller use of an old investment. A town that builds a swimming pool and opens it one hour a day would be laughed at. We do the equivalent with libraries and call it fiscal discipline.

There is also a harder argument beneath the budget debate, and honesty requires naming it. Some opposition to late hours is really discomfort with who uses a library at night: the homeless patron, the noisy teenager, the person who seems to be there mostly for the warmth. That discomfort is understandable, and librarians deal with real behavioral challenges. But the answer to a public space serving the whole public is not to close it. It is to staff it properly, set clear rules, and accept that an institution open to everyone will, in fact, be used by everyone. A library empty of difficult people is usually a library empty of people.

A town tells you what it values by what it keeps lit after dark. We find money to keep stadiums glowing, highways plowed, and offices humming. A reading room with students in it deserves the same commitment. The library at nine in the evening is not a burden on the community. It is the community, doing quietly and without fanfare the thing a community is supposed to do: holding the door open for whoever walks through it.

Turn the lights on, and leave them on.

## Why a cluster needs one leader

Raft keeps a set of servers agreeing on a single log of commands. To make that manageable, Raft designates exactly one server as the leader. Clients talk only to the leader, the leader appends entries to its log, and it replicates those entries to the followers. If any follower could accept writes, replicas would diverge. Election is the mechanism the cluster uses to pick that one leader, and to replace it when it fails.

## Terms: a logical clock

Raft divides time into terms. A term is an integer that increases monotonically, and each term has at most one leader [RAFT]. Think of a term as a presidency: it begins with an election, and it lasts until that leader crashes, gets partitioned away, or is deposed by a higher term.

Every server stores its `currentTerm` durably on disk. Servers exchange their term in every RPC. The rule is simple:

- If you receive a message with a higher term than yours, you step down to follower and adopt the higher term.
- If you receive a message with a lower term, you reject it.

This term check is how Raft resolves confusion after network partitions. A server isolated in an old term cannot fool the rest of the cluster once it rejoins, because everyone else has moved to a newer term and will ignore it.

## The three states

At any moment a server is in one of three states:

```
            times out,          receives votes
            starts election     from majority
follower ──────────────► candidate ──────────────► leader
   ▲                        │                        │
   │                        │ discovers higher       │ discovers
   └────────────────────────┤ term or new leader     │ higher term
                            ▼                        │
                      follower ◄─────────────────────┘
```

- **Follower**: passive. It answers requests from leaders and candidates and accepts log entries.
- **Candidate**: actively asking for votes after an election timeout fired.
- **Leader**: sending heartbeats and log entries, handling client requests.

The normal steady state is one leader and the rest followers. Transitions happen only through timeouts and RPCs, never through some external coordinator.

## Heartbeats: the leader's lease on power

A leader does not hold office through a lease file or a lock. It holds office by staying in contact. The leader sends periodic `AppendEntries` RPCs to every follower. When these carry no log entries, they are called heartbeats [RAFT].

Heartbeats serve two jobs. First, they replicate the log. Second, and more important for election, they reset each follower's election timer. As long as a follower keeps hearing from a leader with a current term, it has no reason to start an election. Silence is the trigger.

The heartbeat interval is much shorter than the election timeout. In the original paper's reference implementation the leader sends heartbeats roughly every 50 ms, while election timeouts sit in the 150 to 300 ms range [RAFT]. That gap means a single dropped packet does not cause a leadership change; the follower waits several missed heartbeats before acting.

## Election timeouts: how a challenge starts

Every follower runs a randomized election timer. If the timer expires without a valid heartbeat or log append, the follower concludes the leader is gone and starts an election:

1. Increment `currentTerm`.
2. Transition to candidate.
3. Vote for itself.
4. Send `RequestVote` RPCs to all other servers.
5. Reset its own election timer (the election itself must also complete within a timeout).

A candidate becomes leader when it receives votes from a majority of the cluster. In a five-node cluster that means three votes. Each server votes for at most one candidate per term, and it votes on a first-come, first-served basis [RAFT]. The majority requirement is the safety core of Raft: two majorities in the same term must overlap in at least one server, and that server can vote only once, so two leaders cannot win the same term.

Candidates also include their last log index and term in the `RequestVote` RPC. A voter denies its vote if the candidate's log is older than its own. This guarantees the winner holds every committed entry, which is why Raft never needs to copy committed entries backwards from followers to a new leader.

## Split votes and randomization

What if two followers time out at nearly the same moment? Both become candidates, each votes for itself, and the remaining votes divide. With an even split, nobody reaches a majority. That is a split vote, and the term ends with no leader.

Split votes are not a correctness problem; they are a liveness problem. If timeouts were fixed, two servers that started elections together once would do it again every round, and the cluster could stall indefinitely. Raft solves this with randomization: each server's election timeout is drawn from a range, not a constant [RAFT]. After a failed election, the candidates draw fresh random timeouts. The probability that the same collision repeats shrinks fast, so a leader usually emerges within one or two rounds.

This is the detail junior engineers most often get wrong when reimplementing Raft: they use a fixed timeout, and their test cluster deadlocks in repeated split votes. Randomize, every round.

## Putting it together

The full cycle in one paragraph: followers listen. Heartbeats keep them quiet. Silence starts an election in a new term. A majority vote, filtered by log freshness, crowns a leader. Randomized timeouts guarantee that contested elections resolve quickly. The result is a cluster that always has at most one leader per term, recovers from a leader crash within a few hundred milliseconds, and never requires manual intervention to pick a replacement.

When you debug a Raft-based system (etcd, Consul, TiKV), most leader-election mysteries reduce to these knobs: clock skew stretching timers, network latency eating the heartbeat budget, or a misconfigured timeout range causing constant re-elections. Check the terms in the logs first; they tell you who believed what, and when.

## References

The bell over the door rang. Marisol looked up from the truing stand.

"Morning. What can I do for you?"

"It's my bike. There's something wrong with it."

"Okay. What kind of something?"

The customer set a hand on the saddle of a gray hybrid and rolled it forward. "It's hard to explain."

"Try me. I've heard everything."

"It makes a noise."

"What kind of noise?"

"A weird one."

Marisol waited.

"Like a... a tick. No. A knock. A ticky knock."

"A ticky knock."

"Yeah. But not all the time."

"When does it happen?"

"When I'm riding it."

"That's a start. When you're pedaling? Coasting? Braking?"

The customer frowned at the ceiling. "Pedaling, I think. Mostly."

"Mostly."

"Well, when I pedal hard. Like up the hill on Foster. It goes tick, tick, tick. Or knock. But then sometimes on the flat it does it too, so maybe it's not the pedaling."

"Does it happen when you stand up on the pedals?"

"Stand up?"

"Out of the saddle. Sprint a little."

"I don't sprint."

"Humor me. On the way home, stand up and pedal. If the noise goes away, that tells us something."

"I won't remember by the time I get home."

Marisol pulled a sticky note off the register and wrote on it. She stuck it to the top tube. "There. Homework."

"Can't you just look at it?"

"I can. That's the plan." She lifted the bike into the stand and spun the crank by hand. The chain moved clean over the rings. "When did it start?"

"A while ago."

"Last week? Last year?"

"Somewhere in there. It got worse after I took it to the beach."

"The beach."

"Yeah. It fell over in the sand."

"Okay. That helps." She spun the rear wheel. "Anything else happen to it? Bumps, drops, a roommate backing over it with a car?"

"No. Well. It fell off the rack once."

"Off a car rack?"

"Onto the driveway. But that was before the noise. I think. Actually it might've been after. Does it matter?"

"It all matters. Order matters less than you'd think." She squeezed the rear brake lever, then the front. "Does the noise speed up when you go faster?"

"Maybe? It's hard to hear over the wind and stuff."

"What about when you turn?"

"I don't think so. Wait. Yes. No. Only left turns."

"Only left turns."

"Pretty sure."

"How sure?"

"Forty percent?"

Marisol turned the handlebars and crouched by the front hub. She plucked a spoke. Then another. "Has anyone worked on it recently?"

"My brother-in-law tightened some stuff."

"Which stuff?"

"The stuff that was loose. He said the crank was loose, so he tightened it. He has tools."

"Does the noise happen once per pedal stroke, or randomly?"

"Per pedal... what does that mean?"

"Every time your right foot comes around, tick. Or just whenever it feels like it."

"Oh. Whenever it feels like it. It's got a mind of its own."

"Bikes usually do what physics tells them. People are the unpredictable part." She flipped the bike's kickstand down, then back up. It rattled. She looked at it. She flicked it with one finger. Tick.

"Huh."

"What?"

She grabbed the crank arm and pushed it side to side. A faint click, barely there. "Bottom bracket's got some play. And your kickstand bolt is loose enough to dance."

"Is the dancing the ticky knock?"

"The kickstand is one noise. The bottom bracket is another. You might have a whole percussion section in here."

"That's bad?"

"That's fixable. Sand doesn't help. Falls don't help. Your brother-in-law's enthusiasm didn't help."

"He meant well."

"They always do." She pulled the chain off the ring and flexed it. Two links stuck at an angle like a bent finger. "And here. Stiff links. This is your tick, most likely. The knock is the bottom bracket. The kickstand is the free bonus track."

"So you found it? Without me even describing it right?"

"You described it fine. Tick versus knock, worse uphill, maybe left turns. That's more than I usually get. Last week a guy told me his bike felt, quote, emotionally off."

"Emotionally off?"

"He needed air in his tires."

The customer laughed. "So what's the damage?"

"Chain clean and lube, tighten the bottom bracket, kickstand bolt. Forty minutes. Call it sixty bucks. If the bracket's shot, add thirty and a day."

"Do it." The customer peeled the sticky note off the top tube. "Guess I don't need this."

"Keep it. Stand up on the hill anyway. If it still ticks after all this, I want to know."

"And if it ticks when I stand?"

"Then it's your knees, and I can't help you."

Marisol wheeled the bike toward the back. "Coffee shop next door. Come back in an hour."

"How will I know it's fixed?"

"You'll know. It'll be the quietest ride of your life."

"It was never that loud."

"It never is," Marisol said. "Until it is."

The ferry left the dock at 11:40 with nine cars and a handful of passengers, most of them asleep in their vehicles. Ruth had chosen to ride up top because her car smelled of the casserole dish she had forgotten in the trunk for two days, and the cold was a better companion than that.

The deck was nearly empty. A man in a high-visibility vest smoked by the stern railing, facing away. Near the bow, a bench ran along the cabin wall under a row of windows that glowed a flat, tired yellow, and on it sat a woman with a paper coffee cup held in both hands like a small animal she was keeping warm.

Ruth hesitated. The whole deck was open. Sitting beside a stranger at midnight on the water was the kind of thing her daughter would call unnecessary. But the bench was the only seat out of the wind, and her knees were not what they had been. She sat at the far end.

"Mind the middle," the woman said, without looking over. "It's wet. The seam drips."

"Thank you." Ruth shifted her bag onto her lap. The woman was younger than her by thirty years, maybe more, with a green wool coat and the kind of boots that cost a week's groceries. She had been crying at some point earlier, Ruth thought, and had stopped, and the stopping had left a stiffness around her mouth.

The engine throbbed through the bench slats. Ahead, the sound was black except for a scatter of lights on the far shore, none of them moving.

"Last one of the night," the woman said. "I didn't know they ran this late."

"Only since the bridge work started. My sister's on the night shift at the hospital over there. I've done this crossing a dozen times this year." Ruth paused. "You're not a regular."

"I missed the nine o'clock." The woman turned the cup a quarter turn in her hands. "Deliberately, if I'm honest. Then I sat in the parking lot for an hour deciding whether that was clever or stupid."

"Which did you land on?"

"Stupid. It's cold." A small exhale that might have been a laugh. "But I'm here, so."

Ruth let the silence sit. She had raised three children and buried a husband, and the main thing she had learned about strangers was that they told you what they needed if you gave them room. The engine note changed as the ferry cleared the breakwater and took the open water, and the deck leaned, gently, like something settling into a chair.

"My mother died this morning," the woman said. "That's why I'm going over. To sort the house. My brother flew in yesterday and started throwing things out before I got there, so now there's that on top of it."

"I'm sorry."

"Thank you." She said it carefully, like a phrase she had been practicing all day and still didn't trust. "Everyone keeps saying it and I keep saying thank you and I don't actually feel anything yet. I feel like I'm doing admin. There's a checklist in my phone. Cancel the paper. Find the will. It's obscene."

"It's not obscene. It's a lifeboat."

The woman looked at her for the first time. Her eyes were red-rimmed but dry. "A lifeboat."

"When my husband went, I ironed. For a week. Everything in the house, sheets, his shirts I was never going to give away yet, tablecloths we hadn't used since the eighties. My daughter thought I'd lost my mind. I hadn't. I just needed my hands to know what to do while the rest of me caught up."

The woman was quiet for a moment. The wake hissed below them. "I keep getting angry at the coffee," she said. "I bought this at the terminal and it's terrible and I was furious about it. Actually furious. Standing there at the machine thinking, she died today and they can't even, what is wrong with this machine."

"That's grief. It goes where it fits."

"Does it ever go where it's supposed to?"

"Not that I've seen."

The woman laughed, a short, cracked sound, and it seemed to surprise her. She wiped her nose with the back of her wrist. "Clare," she said.

"Ruth."

"Ruth." Clare tested it, nodded. "Can I ask you something? Did you ever want to tell people to stop being kind? Because the kind ones are the worst. The pharmacist today. She read the situation off my face in two seconds and her voice went soft and I nearly came apart right there at the counter. I had to buy cough drops I didn't need just to have a reason to stand there a bit longer, and then I left them on the counter. They're probably still there."

"You came apart because she let you. That's a gift, even when it doesn't feel like one."

"It felt like ambush."

"That too," Ruth said. "Both things."

The ferry's horn sounded once, low, and a few seconds later an answering horn came from somewhere out in the dark, a tanker on the shipping lane, patient and enormous. Clare turned her head toward the sound but there was nothing to see, just the black and the running lights winking off the swell.

"She'd have hated this ferry," Clare said. "She got seasick on lake boats. Flat calm, twenty minutes out, green as a pea. But she made my father take her on a dinner cruise every anniversary because she liked the lights on the water. She'd take her tablet and sit where she could see the shore and complain the whole time and then want to go again the next year."

"She knew what she liked."

"She liked complaining about it almost as much." Clare turned the cup again. It had gone quiet between her hands, the warmth spent. "My brother's going to want to sell the house fast. He's a good man, he's not a ghoul, he just wants it done, and I keep thinking, the light in that kitchen at four in the afternoon. Nobody else is going to know about that. Nobody else is going to stand there."

"So stand there," Ruth said. "Before it's done. Take an afternoon and just stand in it. It doesn't fix anything. But you'll have it."

Clare nodded slowly, looking at the far shore. The lights had begun to separate into streets. The ferry was throttling down, the engine's note dropping, and the man in the high-visibility vest had gone below. A gull rode alongside for a stretch and then peeled away.

"Why were you on the nine o'clock?" Ruth asked. "Or not on it."

"The hospital rang at six. She was already gone by then but they waited for my brother to land, they thought family should hear it together, which was kind or wasn't, I still don't know. I got in the car to drive over and I sat in the driveway for forty minutes. And then I missed the ferry. I think I was waiting for someone to tell me I had to go. And nobody did. That's the thing nobody tells you. Nobody comes and makes you."

"No," Ruth said. "They don't. You just find yourself on the last ferry."

Clare looked at her, and this time the smile reached her eyes, briefly, the way a match flares before you cup it. "On a wet bench. Avoiding the seam."

"Avoiding the seam."

The ramp clanged somewhere below and a voice came over the loudspeaker, distorted and gentle, announcing the arrival. Clare stood and dropped her cup in the bin by the cabin door, then stood there a moment with her hand still on the lid, as if the motion had cost her something.

"Come on," Ruth said, getting up, her knees complaining. "I'll walk you down. The stairs are steep and the handrail's cold. You'll want to know that."

They went down together, slowly, one flight behind the last of the sleepy drivers. At the car deck Clare turned and squeezed Ruth's forearm once, quickly, the way you touch a doorframe on your way out of a room, and then she was gone toward a silver hatchback three rows over.

Ruth found her own car and sat in it while the deckhands waved the line forward. The casserole smell had faded. She drove off into the sparse midnight traffic and followed the taillights ahead of her over the rise of the coast road, and for a while one particular pair of them stayed in front, all the way to the hospital turnoff, where they went one way and she went the other.

The config file has no `[[harbour]]` blocks, or tidewatch read a different file than you expect. Run `tidewatch once --config /path/to/config.toml` to confirm the path. Run `tidewatch doctor` to print the resolved config path and the parsed harbour list.

**`error: authentication failed (401)`**
The API key is missing or wrong. Check `TIDEWATCH_API_KEY` and the `api_key` value in the config. WorldTides keys expire after a year; request a new one from the provider console.

**Times are off by one hour**
The `timezone` value does not match your location, or it is not a valid IANA name. Use `Europe/London`, not `GMT`. Run `tidewatch doctor` to see the resolved timezone.

**`error: rate limit exceeded (429)`**
The provider rejected too many requests. Raise `cache_ttl` so tidewatch reuses tide tables longer, or raise the watch `--interval`. NOAA allows about five requests per minute per key.

**Blank table in watch mode**
The terminal does not support screen clearing, or output is piped. Watch mode needs an interactive terminal. Use `tidewatch once` in a loop instead:

```bash
while true; do tidewatch once; sleep 300; done
```

**Stale data after a station change**
The cache holds the old table. Delete the cache directory `~/.cache/tidewatch` or wait for `cache_ttl` to expire.

## Corvid Q3 review: strong sound, honest price

Corvid is not a household name, and the Q3 is only the third pair of over-ear wireless headphones the company has made. After two weeks of daily use on trains, at a desk, and on long walks, I can say this: the Q3 is a serious pair of headphones that costs less than it should.

### Sound

The Q3 uses 40mm dynamic drivers, and Corvid tuned them with restraint. The bass has weight without swallowing the midrange. Kick drums hit with a satisfying thump on electronic tracks, but vocals stay in front of the mix instead of drowning in low end. On acoustic recordings, guitars sound like wood and string, not like a synthesizer's idea of a guitar.

The treble is the one area where the tuning shows a slight preference for safety. Cymbals and hi-hats sound a touch rolled off, which makes long listening sessions easy on the ears but takes some sparkle out of brighter tracks. I noticed this most on jazz recordings, where a ride cymbal lost some of its shimmer. Most listeners will not care. Audiophiles with a careful ear might.

The soundstage is wider than I expected at this price. Instruments have room to breathe, and you can place a drummer behind and slightly to the left of a vocalist. It will not match a pair of open-back wired headphones, but for a closed wireless design it does well.

Active noise cancellation is competent rather than class-leading. It erases the low rumble of a train and the drone of an air conditioner almost completely. Higher-frequency sounds, like a colleague's keyboard clatter or a crying baby two rows back, get softened rather than removed. The transparency mode sounds natural enough for a quick conversation, though your own voice comes through slightly muffled.

### Comfort

At 254 grams, the Q3 sits in the comfortable middle of the weight range. The headband spreads pressure evenly, and the memory foam earpads are deep enough that my ears never touch the driver housing. I wore them for a four-hour stretch of writing and forgot they were on, which is the highest compliment I can give a pair of headphones.

Clamping force is on the gentle side. That is good news for glasses wearers, since the arms of my frames caused no hotspots. The tradeoff is that the Q3 shifts if you lean forward sharply or try to wear them during a workout. These are desk, commute, and couch headphones, not gym headphones.

The earpads run a little warm after an hour in a stuffy room. Nothing extreme, but on a summer day you will notice.

### Battery

Corvid claims 40 hours with noise cancellation on, and my testing came close. I averaged 37 hours across three full charge cycles at moderate volume. That puts the Q3 ahead of several competitors that cost twice as much.

A 10-minute charge over USB-C gives you roughly five hours of playback, which saved me twice when I forgot to plug in overnight. A full charge takes just under two hours. The Q3 also works passively with the included 3.5mm cable if the battery dies, though noise cancellation and the on-board controls stop working in wired mode.

### Value

Here is where the Q3 gets interesting. At $179, it undercuts the big-name flagships by a wide margin while matching them on battery life and getting most of the way there on sound and noise cancellation. The companion app is basic but functional, with a five-band equalizer and firmware update support. Build quality feels sturdy, with metal hinges and a folding design that fits into the included hard case.

Run these steps in order. Each step takes under two minutes.

**Step 1: Identify the lagging replica.** The alert names the instance. Confirm from the primary:

```sql
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn,
       now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

Compare `sent_lsn` against `replay_lsn`. If `sent_lsn` is current but `replay_lsn` is behind, the replica receives WAL but cannot apply it. If `sent_lsn` itself is behind, the problem is upstream of the replica [PGDOCS-MON].

**Step 2: Check whether the receiver and WAL sender are alive.** On the replica:

```sql
SELECT status, receive_start_lsn, written_lsn, flushed_lsn
FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver;
```

If this returns no rows, streaming has stopped entirely. Go to cause: replication slot or WAL sender failure [PGDOCS-RECV].

**Step 3: Check for replay conflicts.** On the replica:

```sql
SELECT datname, confl_lock, confl_snapshot, confl_bufferpin, confl_deadlock
FROM pg_stat_database_conflicts;
```

Rising counters, especially `confl_lock` or `confl_snapshot`, mean a query on the replica blocks replay. Go to cause: long-running query on the replica [PGDOCS-CONF].

**Step 4: Check WAL volume.** Compare the lag trend against write traffic:

```sql
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS lag_bytes
FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

Large `lag_bytes` during a bulk load, backfill, or index build points to cause: write burst exceeds apply capacity.

The envelopes arrive in bundles now, like something washed ashore. Bills, catalogs, a coupon for gutter cleaning. But sometimes, buried in the pile, there is one with handwriting on it, and my whole posture changes before I have even registered why. The pen pressed too hard in places. A crossed-out word. The stamp slightly crooked. Someone sat down for me.

That is the whole of it, probably, but it deserves a slower look.

A letter is slow in a way that almost nothing else in our lives is slow anymore. The writer cannot delete. If you change your mind mid-sentence, the evidence stays, a small strikethrough that says: I thought one thing, then I thought another, and I let you see both. Email flatters us into believing our first draft is our finished self. A handwritten letter admits the drafts were the self. My grandmother's letters from the 1970s are full of these seams. In the margins she wrote grocery lists. On the back of one she traced her hand, spread wide, so I could compare mine against hers at age eight. No formatting menu offers that.

There is also the matter of the hand itself. We have nearly lost the ability to recognize each other this way. For centuries, you could pick out a friend's handwriting across a crowded post office, the way you now pick out their walk or their laugh. My father writes in cramped capital letters, never cursive, because a teacher in 1962 told him his lowercase was disgraceful, and he decided, at nine, never to risk it again. I know this because he told me, but I also know it because every birthday card he has sent carries the scar of that classroom. Typography has no grudges. Handwriting is nothing but grudges, and pressure, and the particular fatigue of a wrist on a Tuesday.

Some people say they write letters because letters get kept. This is true in a way that is hard to overstate. My family has a shoebox containing a letter my great-grandfather sent from a lumber camp in 1911, four sentences long, informing his wife that the winter was " tolerable" and enclosing two dollars. Nobody in the family keeps texts. The medium itself makes the argument: this survived a century in a box under stairs, through floods and moves and indifference, because paper asks nothing. It needs no password, no operating system, no company that stays in business. You hold it up to a lamp and it works. A letter is the only message we send that does not depend on the sender still existing, or the infrastructure still running, or anyone remembering to pay for storage.

But I don't think permanence is really why the letter writers I know keep doing it. I think it is the obligation of the body. To write by hand is to spend something measurable: fifteen minutes, an ache in the knuckles, half a sheet of good paper you were saving. The recipient feels the spending. It is the difference between being handed a gift and being handed a receipt for a gift. When my friend Marcus was going through a divorce, he told me he received ninety texts and three letters, and that he reread the letters and never reread the texts. He could not explain it except to say the letters "took up room." They took up room in the envelope, on his nightstand, in his sense of what he was worth to people. Weight, literally.

There is a privacy to it that we have forgotten how to name. A letter passes from one hand to one hand. It is not scanned for keywords, not summarized by a machine, not surfaced at an anniversary by a service hoping to sell photo books. It is addressed, deliberately, to a single reader, and everyone else in the world is excluded by the physics of paper. In an era when nearly every act of communication is also an act of publication, performed on a stage owned by somebody else, the letter is one of the last rooms with a door. My mother wrote letters to her sister for fifty years, and when the sister died, the letters came back to her in a crate. She has not reread them. She says she does not need to; she knows what is in them; that is what writing them was for.

And there is the delay, which we treat as a defect and which is the point. Between the writing and the reading sits a stretch of days during which the writer's mood settles, the news ages, and the sentences do their slow work without the writer hovering. You cannot ask a letter "did you see this?" or watch the typing dots pulse. The letter goes out like a message in a bottle: thrown sincerely, aimed loosely, arriving whenever. Some of the best letters I have received answered questions I had stopped needing answered and raised ones I had not yet thought to ask. The slowness creates a strange intimacy across time. You are alone with someone who was recently alone, thinking of you.

None of this makes the handwritten letter superior, exactly. It is inefficient, bad for the wrists, environmentally expensive, and often illegible. My grandfather's last letters to me were shaky enough that I had to hold them at arm's length and guess. But those guesses are now among the things I own. I would not trade them for a clearer recording of his voice, though I have that too, on a phone I no longer own, in a file I cannot open.

So the people who still write by hand are not being nostalgic, or not only. They are insisting that some communications should cost the sender something visible, and should reach only one person, and should carry the marks of the hours they were written in: the smudge, the cramped capitals, the grocery list, the traced hand. A letter is proof that a body sat somewhere and thought of you, at length, without interruption, on paper that will still open a hundred years from now, in a lamp's plain light, no matter what becomes of us.
